slides.title: The first conversation
slides.lead: Day 2 · Handling a Zillow Preferred lead with confidence
slides.body:
From the first hello
to a useful next step.

Learn the lead routes. Choose the right response. Guide the call with ALMS.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: Eric’s September 14 Day 2 objective.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: What we’ll cover
slides.lead: Learn a piece, see an example, then try it.
slides.body:
1. Recognize the lead

    What the buyer requested, how it arrived, and what needs confirming.

  2. Start the conversation

    Live connections, outbound calls, texts, and requested callbacks.

  3. Use ALMS

    Appointment, Location, Motivation, and Summarize—with questions that follow the buyer’s answers.

  4. Put it together

    Handle common turns, complete the call, and follow through.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: September 14 objective.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Help them take the next step
slides.lead: A request to see a home is interest in seeing it—not a promise to buy it.
slides.body:
Make meeting easy

Introduce yourself, help with the request, and offer a useful appointment early.

Understand the person

Learn what drew them to the home and why those details matter.

Earn the next conversation

Give helpful answers and a clear plan. Success can include a buyer choosing to wait.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R001–R002, R013, R024.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Three lead routes
slides.lead: Read the lead’s type and actual request before choosing your response.
slides.body:
Lead typeBuyer requestHow it reaches you
Connection / contact agentContact about a home for saleLive phone connection or FUB alert with contact preference
Real-time touringA tour, using availability supplied through ShowingTimeFUB alert; not a live call in TRU’s documented flow
Standard property tourA tour at a requested timeLive connection or FUB alert; requested time may still need availability checks
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: INT-012; documented TRU operating flow.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Read what they actually sent
slides.lead: A few details tell you how to begin.
slides.body:
Request + property

Did they ask for information, agent contact, or a tour? Use the actual home and request in your opening.

Time + channel

Check the requested tour time, callback time, or “text me first” preference. Those are different instructions.

Buyer context

Use the timeframe and any supplied agreement answer. A question on an intake form does not tell you how this buyer answered.

A requested time, confirmed property access, and a completed showing are three different things.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: INT-012–INT-013.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: A tour request still needs your help
slides.lead: Real-time touring supplies a stronger starting point for scheduling.
slides.body:
Real-time touring

The displayed slots draw on ShowingTime / MLS availability supplied by the seller or listing agent. Read the requested slot and verify the current arrangements.

Standard tour request

Where that availability is not integrated, a displayed time can be a buyer request rather than available access. Check before promising it.

Your response

Acknowledge the requested time. Tell the buyer what is confirmed and what you are checking. Do not make them start over.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: INT-012.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Read the request
slides.lead: A standard tour lead asks for 5 p.m. The property’s availability is not confirmed. What do you do?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Acknowledge 5 p.m., check access, and tell the buyer when you will confirm. Their request gives you a starting point; it does not prove the seller approved it.

Use the requested time while keeping an unverified arrangement separate from a confirmed appointment.
slides.notes: Let agents answer before revealing the explanation. Discuss their reasoning without treating a short answer as proof of live-call skill. In self-paced study, use the reveal to compare your answer and revisit the preceding lesson. Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction.
slides.cue: What led you to that answer?

activity.prompt: A standard tour lead asks for 5 p.m. The property’s availability is not confirmed. What do you do?

choices.text: Acknowledge 5 p.m. and verify property access.
Tell them the showing is confirmed because they selected 5 p.m.
Ignore 5 p.m. and ask when they want to tour.

slides.title: Choose the response that fits
slides.lead: Calls help you hear tone, ask follow-up questions, and build a relationship.
slides.body:
Already connected live

Begin the conversation. You already have the buyer on the phone; no separate outbound call is needed.

New alert, no special preference

Call within five minutes of receiving it in TRU’s normal 8 a.m.–8 p.m. operating window. Automation does not replace your call.

A stated preference

Honor text-first and requested callback instructions. An explicit “do not call” request is a boundary to respect.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R008–R010; INT-009–INT-013, INT-054.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: If the first call is unanswered
slides.lead: Make it easy for the buyer to recognize you and respond.
slides.body:
1. Call promptly

    Place the call within five minutes of receipt in the normal flow. Leave an opening voicemail when appropriate.

  2. Follow with a personal text

    Connect to the real inquiry and invite a phone conversation with genuine availability.

  3. Keep ownership

    Continue useful outreach while unanswered. The automated introduction is separate from your work.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R009, R019.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: “Text now” and “call at five”
slides.lead: Acknowledge the buyer now while respecting the plan they requested.
slides.body:
“Text is better right now.”

“Of course. I can help here. A quick call would also let us talk through the home and your plans—would this evening work?” Text now; do not record a permanent no-call preference.

“Call me at five.”

“Hi Maya, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, the agent who’ll call at five about your request. Let me know if you have questions before then.” Keep five unless the buyer agrees to change it.

“Please do not call me.”

Honor that request. Give useful help through the agreed channel.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R008, R010; INT-013, INT-043.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Choose your next message
slides.lead: Maya’s alert arrives at 2 p.m. and asks for a 5 p.m. call. Write your acknowledgment.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Hi Maya, I’m Sam with Northside Realty. I’ll be calling at five about your inquiry. If you have a question before then, let me know. I’m also free earlier if that would help.

Introduce yourself promptly, keep the requested call time, and offer earlier availability only if it is real. Do not call immediately just to satisfy the normal five-minute default.

slides.title: ALMS is your call framework
slides.lead: Start with a clear introduction. Then help with the appointment before discovery.
slides.body:
A

Appointment

Make it easy to meet.

L

Location

Understand where and what fits.

M

Motivation

Learn why it matters.

S

Summarize

Confirm what happens next.

Location and motivation can flow in either order. Listen to the person; do not recite a checklist.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R012–R013; INT-015–INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Take the first turn
slides.lead: Orient the buyer: your name, brokerage, Zillow connection, and reason for the conversation.
slides.body:
Live connection

“Zillow connected us about your request…” fits a buyer already on the line. Begin warmly instead of waiting in silence.

Outbound call

“I’m calling about your request…” connects an unfamiliar number to something the buyer recognizes.

Use your real brokerage and role. Do not borrow claims about expertise or relationships that are not yours.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: A · Appointment
slides.lead: Help with the reason they reached out before asking them to complete your process.
slides.body:
When no time is requested

Offer two genuine options: “Would this afternoon or tomorrow morning work better?” Check property access before confirming.

Why it comes early

The buyer asked for help. An early invitation makes that help tangible; a long qualification interview can make the meeting feel conditional.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R001, R013; INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Now try the opening
slides.lead: Jordan asked to see 1234 Lane and has not requested a time. How would you begin?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about your request to see 1234 Lane. Would Saturday morning or afternoon work better? I’ll verify access for the time we choose.

Orient the buyer and offer useful times before discovery. Use actual availability. The invitation is a strong default, not a reason to ignore a buyer’s stated circumstances.
slides.notes: Let agents answer before revealing the explanation. Discuss their reasoning without treating a short answer as proof of live-call skill. In self-paced study, use the reveal to compare your answer and revisit the preceding lesson. Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction.
slides.cue: What led you to that answer?

fields.label: Write your introduction and early appointment invitation.

activity.model: Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about your request to see 1234 Lane. Would Saturday morning or afternoon work better? I’ll verify access for the time we choose.
activity.explanation: Orient the buyer and offer useful times before discovery. Use actual availability. The invitation is a strong default, not a reason to ignore a buyer’s stated circumstances.

choices.text: Introduce yourself and offer workable showing times.
Start by asking for preapproval and budget.
Explain the entire buying process first.

slides.title: Ask for a few minutes
slides.lead: Explain why the questions will help the buyer.
slides.body:
If they have time

Ask one question, listen, and use the answer to choose the next question.

If they are rushed

“Absolutely—let’s keep this quick.” Handle the appointment and essentials. Do not force the buyer through every question.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016, INT-023.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: L · Location
slides.lead: Learn where the buyer wants to be—and what makes it work for them.
slides.body:
Start with their search

“What attracted you to this area?” or “Are there other areas you’re considering?”

Understand the connection

“What would make this location convenient for you?” Let the buyer explain the priorities.

Use what you already know

If they said they are moving from nearby, ask what is changing where they live now rather than repeating the intake form.

Location includes more than a ZIP code. Let the buyer define the places, routines, and tradeoffs that matter.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016, INT-021.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: M · Motivation
slides.lead: Move from the feature to the reason behind it.
slides.body:
Buyer “We really want a bigger yard.”

Agent “What would you like to be able to do with that space?”

Buyer “I want room for a vegetable garden.”

Agent “That helps. What would the garden need from the space?”

“Big yard” is a feature. Gardening gives it meaning. Do not assume dogs, children, entertaining, or any other reason.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016, INT-021.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Stay with the answer
slides.lead: A conversation learns something. An interrogation just collects fields.
slides.body:
Acknowledge

Respond to what they said: “That makes sense—you want space you can actually use.”

Ask a relevant follow-up

“What is missing in your current place?” or “What would make the move worthwhile?”

Use the answer

Choose the next question or property comparison from that information. Warmth comes from attention, not a memorized joke.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-021.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Ask the next question
slides.lead: The buyer says, “We’re already in town. We just need more space.”
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“What is feeling too tight in your current place?” Their answer could reveal the purpose of the space. Follow that answer rather than assuming a larger bedroom count solves it.

Choose a question connected to the buyer’s words. There is no required question count, personal anecdote, or fixed order for location and motivation.
slides.notes: Let agents answer before revealing the explanation. Discuss their reasoning without treating a short answer as proof of live-call skill. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction.

slides.title: Make the outing useful
slides.lead: Propose two or three homes so the buyer can compare and you can learn their preferences.
slides.body:
Explain the value

Comparisons help the buyer clarify what fits. They also give you options if one property becomes unavailable.

Respect the answer

Do not make extra homes a condition for seeing the original one. Be honest when an option differs from their criteria.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R012, R021; INT-015, INT-037–INT-039.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: S · Summarize
slides.lead: Give the buyer back their priorities and the agreed next step.
slides.body: Name what is agreed, what still needs checking, and who will do it. Invite the buyer to correct you.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Before you hang up
slides.lead: A good close removes uncertainty.
slides.body:
Appointment details

Restate the day, time, property or meeting location, and any access check still outstanding.

What they will receive

Explain the applicable touring form briefly and accurately. Confirm what you will send and when you will follow up.

What you will do

Research promised answers and comparisons. Save the buyer’s priorities and agreed next action in FUB.

If a form or existing agreement raises a question you cannot resolve, call your team lead. Use the actual form’s terms.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013, R015–R016, R021.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Close this call
slides.lead: Jordan wants garden space, prefers Saturday morning, and is open to another home. Access is still unconfirmed.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“The garden space is important, and Saturday morning is your preference. I’ll check access and find another useful comparison. I’ll send the confirmed details after I hear back. Is there anything I missed?”

Do not upgrade a requested time into a confirmed showing. Reflect the actual priorities and your promised action.

Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction.

slides.title: “I just have questions.”
slides.lead: Help with the question; earn another invitation through useful service.
slides.body:
1. Acknowledge and capture

    “Of course—what would you like to know?” Answer accurately; say what you need to check.

  2. Learn the context

    With permission, understand what drew them to the home and how the answer affects their search.

  3. Offer a useful next step

    Explain how seeing the home could help. If they still decline, stop pushing and agree how you’ll bring back the answers.

Answers are not a reward for agreeing to a showing. Never guess or hide a known answer.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R014; INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Keep the first meeting easy
slides.lead: Do not open with a demand for preapproval, budget, or proof they are ready to buy.
slides.body:
Why timing matters

They asked to see a home. A private financial interview from someone they do not know can turn that request into a barrier.

If the buyer asks

Answer their question. Learn enough context to make guidance useful; involve a lender for financing specifics.

The usual later opening

The end of the first showing offers context for a relevant financing conversation. A long buying timeline does not automatically rule out planning help.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R001–R004; INT-001–INT-005, INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Respond to their question
slides.lead: The buyer asks, “Should I talk to a lender before we look?” What is the best response?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“Happy to help. What timing do you have in mind for a move?” Use the context to explain a useful next step and offer lender help where it fits.

Buyer-initiated financing questions deserve an answer. Avoid both a blanket refusal to discuss money and a blanket requirement to obtain preapproval before receiving help.
slides.notes: Let agents answer before revealing the explanation. Discuss their reasoning without treating a short answer as proof of live-call skill. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction.

choices.text: Understand their timing and concern, then offer relevant guidance.

slides.title: “Are you the listing agent?”
slides.lead: Answer the role question clearly, then return to how you can help.
slides.body:
If they prefer the listing agent

Offer to help with that connection and ask whether a service check-in would be useful. Respect their decision.

Keep it accurate

Use your real role. Do not imply you represent the seller, invent a relationship, or launch into a full agency lecture.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R015; INT-016–INT-018.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: “Is this home still available?”
slides.lead: If the home is under contract, give the truth and a useful next step.
slides.body:
1. Prepare from their priorities

    Use what they told you to identify relevant alternatives.

  2. Explain what changed

    Say the home is under contract. Offer to check whether viewing or another option is still possible; do not promise it.

  3. Keep the next step useful

    Learn what drew them to this home and offer a relevant option to explore together. Let the buyer decide.

Do not end the conversation with a bare “It’s under contract. Want something else?” Ask what mattered and explain what you can check.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R011–R012 applied to the initial availability question.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Keep helping with the inquiry
slides.lead: On the first call, Jordan asks about a home that is under contract. You learn garden space matters. What do you say?
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

“The home is under contract. I can check whether a viewing is still possible. Since garden space matters, I can also research some options to compare. Would that be useful?” Keep access and unresearched alternatives conditional.

Tell the truth, use known priorities, keep possibilities conditional, and offer a next step. Do not merely hand the search back with “Want something else?”

Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: TRU Sales Proccess; application of the preceding instruction.

slides.title: Adapt to the person in front of you
slides.lead: The framework supports judgment.
slides.body:
“I have one minute.”

Keep it quick. Handle the appointment, explain the essential next steps, and respect the time constraint.

“I can’t visit soon.”

Learn the purchase drivers, criteria, and timing. Agree on useful updates and a communication plan instead of forcing a near-term showing.

“I’m not sure buying is right.”

Acknowledge the concern. Ask what is behind it, offer relevant education, and help them decide—even if the decision is to wait.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013, R020, R024; INT-023, INT-035–INT-036, INT-045–INT-050.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: One call, from the opening…
slides.lead: Fictional demonstration · use your own words and true availability.
slides.body:
Introduce “Hi Jordan, I’m Sam with Northside Realty, a featured partner with Zillow. I’m calling about 1234 Lane.”

Appointment “Would Saturday morning or afternoon work better? I’ll verify access.”

Permission “Have you got a few minutes so I can make our outing useful?”

Location “What attracted you to this area?”
Jordan: “It would shorten my commute.”
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R013; adapted from INT-016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: …to a clear next step
slides.lead: The next question comes from what the buyer says.
slides.body:
Motivation “What else caught your eye?”
Jordan: “The yard. I’d like a vegetable garden.”
“What would you need from that space?”

Plan “Would you like to compare a couple of other homes while we’re out?”

Summarize “The commute and garden space matter. Saturday morning is your preference. I’ll check access, research the comparisons, and send the details. Is that right?”

Then briefly explain the applicable touring form and the follow-up you are actually committing to.
slides.notes: Teach the point and its reason, then read the example naturally. Examples use fictional buyers; adapt names, facts, brokerage and availability. Source: R012–R013, R016.
slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: Your turn: handle the whole call
slides.lead: Jordan asked for a tour. Practice the call, then replay one part after feedback.
slides.body:
Compare with the teaching example

Introduce yourself, offer the appointment early, ask permission, explore location and motivation through follow-up questions, and summarize the actual plan. Adapt if Jordan has limited time or a different request.

Use a partner as the buyer. When studying alone, say the agent’s turns aloud and compare with the two demonstration slides. A self-check is practice, not observed coach sign-off.

Rotate agent, buyer and observer so everyone speaks. Give one specific correction and a targeted retry. Do not label a peer or self-check as coach sign-off. Buyer chooses a case from the practice cards; do not hand the agent all the buyer answers in advance.

slides.title: Follow through on what you promised
slides.lead: The next contact should have a reason the buyer recognizes.
slides.body:
Record the useful details

Save the request, location, motivation, communication preference, and agreed plan in FUB. Distinguish requested from confirmed.

Complete the promises

Get the property answer, check access, prepare the comparison, or send the agreed information. Set a task to remember it.

Make the next contact relevant

“I checked the garden space you asked about…” is more useful than an empty “Just checking in.” Use the agreed channel and timing.

slides.cue: What would this change in your next buyer conversation?

slides.title: If the new lead stays unanswered
slides.lead: Continue useful personal outreach; do not confuse automation with your effort.
slides.body:
Day one

Aim for three to four personal touches. The stated minimum is two calls and one personal text in the normal unanswered-lead flow.

First week

Aim for ten total touches, including day one. Most attempts should be calls; use relevant texts and vary contact times.

When they respond

Follow the conversation and agreed plan. Stop applying the unanswered-lead quota. An explicit contact restriction still governs.

If an engaged buyer later goes quiet, keep making thoughtful attempts. The stopping point is discretionary; there is no fixed new quota.

slides.body:

ALMS: Appointment, Location, Motivation, Summarize. Introduce yourself first. Offer useful help early, honor stated contact preferences, and follow the buyer’s answers instead of collecting a checklist.
